claim: Cortical plasticity is fundamental to motor recovery following cortical perturbation.
source: Cortical plasticity is fundamental to motor recovery following cortical perturbation.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that draws from established scientific understanding about cortical plasticity and motor recovery.

claim: Optogenetic unilateral suppression of a portion of the secondary motor cortex (MOs) that encodes contraversive eye movement severely impaired contraversive movement on the first day.
source: Optogenetic unilateral suppression severely impaired contraversive movement on the first day.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, specifically in Figure 2 and related text.

claim: On subsequent days after optogenetic suppression, the suppression became inefficient and capability for the movement was restored.
source: However, on subsequent days the suppression became inefficient and capability for the movement was restored.
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 2C and related behavioral data.

claim: The regained capability for contraversive eye movement was accompanied by an increased number of neurons encoding for ipsiversive movement in the unsuppressed contralateral MOs.
source: Longitudinal two-photon calcium imaging revealed that the regained capability was accompanied by an increased number of neurons encoding for ipsiversive movement in the unsuppressed contralateral MOs.
evidence: This is supported by two-photon calcium imaging data presented in Figure 3.

claim: Additional suppression of the contralateral MOs impaired the recovered movement again.
source: Additional suppression of the contralateral MOs impaired the recovered movement again, indicating a compensatory mechanism.
evidence: This is supported by bilateral suppression experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: Repeated optogenetic suppression leads to functional recovery mediated by the contralateral hemisphere.
source: Our findings demonstrate that repeated optogenetic suppression leads to functional recovery mediated by the contralateral hemisphere.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Neural plasticity in motor cortex is critical for motor learning.
source: Neural plasticity in motor cortex is critical not only for motor learning (Peters et al., 2017), but also for motor recovery following cortical damage (Nudo, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Peters et al., 2017.

claim: Neural plasticity in motor cortex is critical for motor recovery following cortical damage.
source: Neural plasticity in motor cortex is critical not only for motor learning (Peters et al., 2017), but also for motor recovery following cortical damage (Nudo, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Nudo, 2013.

claim: Motor plasticity has been traditionally investigated using motor cortex in higher animals.
source: Motor plasticity has been traditionally investigated using motor cortex in higher animals (Travis and Woolsey, 1956).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Travis and Woolsey, 1956.

claim: Recent technical advancements have rendered rodent cortex a fruitful model to study circuit mechanisms in motor learning.
source: However, recent technical advancements have rendered rodent cortex a fruitful model to study circuit mechanisms in motor learning (Makino et al., 2016), motor deficits (Ebbesen and Brecht, 2017) and motor recovery (Murphy and Corbett, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Makino et al., 2016.

claim: Recent technical advancements have rendered rodent cortex a fruitful model to study motor deficits.
source: However, recent technical advancements have rendered rodent cortex a fruitful model to study circuit mechanisms in motor learning (Makino et al., 2016), motor deficits (Ebbesen and Brecht, 2017) and motor recovery (Murphy and Corbett, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Ebbesen and Brecht, 2017.

claim: Recent technical advancements have rendered rodent cortex a fruitful model to study motor recovery.
source: However, recent technical advancements have rendered rodent cortex a fruitful model to study circuit mechanisms in motor learning (Makino et al., 2016), motor deficits (Ebbesen and Brecht, 2017) and motor recovery (Murphy and Corbett, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Murphy and Corbett, 2009.

claim: Previous studies in rodents investigated the cellular and molecular mechanisms that underlie compensatory pathophysiological changes in the cortical network during stroke recovery.
source: For example, previous studies in rodents investigated the cellular and molecular mechanisms that underlie compensatory pathophysiological changes in the cortical network during stroke recovery (Alia et al., 2017; Fawcett, 2015; Li et al., 2010; Schwab and Strittmatter, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Compensatory pathophysiological changes during stroke recovery include modification of extracellular matrix structures.
source: Such changes include modification of extracellular matrix structures (Fawcett, 2015) and increased neurotropic factors for angiogenesis, neurogenesis, and synaptic plasticity (Berretta et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Fawcett, 2015.

claim: Compensatory pathophysiological changes during stroke recovery include increased neurotropic factors for angiogenesis, neurogenesis, and synaptic plasticity.
source: Such changes include modification of extracellular matrix structures (Fawcett, 2015) and increased neurotropic factors for angiogenesis, neurogenesis, and synaptic plasticity (Berretta et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Berretta et al., 2014.

claim: It is not clear whether molecular processes are necessary to recover impaired movements or whether motor recovery can be mediated simply by mechanisms similar to motor learning inherent to the physiological circuits.
source: However, it is not clear whether these molecular processes are necessary to recover impaired movements or whether motor recovery can be mediated simply by mechanisms similar to motor learning inherent to the physiological circuits.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in knowledge that the study aims to address.

claim: Recovery from motor deficits relies on the intact brain regions including a hemisphere contralateral to cortical lesions.
source: Recovery from motor deficits relies on the intact brain regions including a hemisphere contralateral to cortical lesions.
evidence: This is a general statement based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: The contralateral hemisphere has been a target for motor rehabilitation in humans.
source: Indeed, the contralateral hemisphere has been a target for motor rehabilitation in humans (Buetefisch, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Buetefisch, 2015.

claim: Eye movement, like binocularly coupled saccade, shows a simple but robust motor output.
source: Eye movement, like binocularly coupled saccade, shows a simple but robust motor output, and its direction is represented mainly in the contralateral frontal cortex.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about eye movement control.

claim: Eye movement direction is represented mainly in the contralateral frontal cortex.
source: Eye movement, like binocularly coupled saccade, shows a simple but robust motor output, and its direction is represented mainly in the contralateral frontal cortex.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about eye movement control.

claim: A unilateral lesion in primate frontal cortex disrupts saccades toward the contralateral side (contraversive saccades).
source: Consistent with this representation, a unilateral lesion in primate frontal cortex disrupts saccades toward the contralateral side (i.e., contraversive saccades) (Crowne et al., 1981; Pierrot-Deseilligny et al., 2002; van der Steen et al., 1986).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple primate studies.

claim: Deficits in contraversive saccades following unilateral frontal cortex lesion can ease over time.
source: However, such deficits can ease over time (Crowne et al., 1981; van der Steen et al., 1986), even after the removal of an entire cortical hemisphere (Bruell and Volk, 1956; Estañol et al., 1980; Herter and Guitton, 2004; Perenin and Jeannerod, 1978; Sharpe et al., 1979; Troost et al., 1972; Tusa et al., 1986).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Crowne et al., 1981 and van der Steen et al., 1986.

claim: Deficits in contraversive saccades can ease even after the removal of an entire cortical hemisphere.
source: However, such deficits can ease over time (Crowne et al., 1981; van der Steen et al., 1986), even after the removal of an entire cortical hemisphere (Bruell and Volk, 1956; Estañol et al., 1980; Herter and Guitton, 2004; Perenin and Jeannerod, 1978; Sharpe et al., 1979; Troost et al., 1972; Tusa et al., 1986).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies on hemispherectomy.

claim: The recovery of the contraversive saccade in primate implies compensatory neural plasticity, potentially involving the contralateral hemisphere.
source: The recovery of the contraversive saccade in primate implies compensatory neural plasticity, potentially involving the contralateral hemisphere.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cited primate studies.

claim: A small portion of the secondary motor cortex (MOs) in the frontal cortex controls contraversive eye movements.
source: Using this task, we previously demonstrated that a small portion of the secondary motor cortex (MOs) in the frontal cortex controls contraversive eye movements, optogenetic suppression of MOs impairs contraversive eye movements, and MOs neurons preferentially encode contraversive eye movements.
evidence: This claim is based on the authors' previous work (Itokazu et al., 2018).

claim: Optogenetic suppression of MOs impairs contraversive eye movements.
source: Using this task, we previously demonstrated that a small portion of the secondary motor cortex (MOs) in the frontal cortex controls contraversive eye movements, optogenetic suppression of MOs impairs contraversive eye movements, and MOs neurons preferentially encode contraversive eye movements.
evidence: This claim is based on the authors' previous work (Itokazu et al., 2018).

claim: MOs neurons preferentially encode contraversive eye movements.
source: Using this task, we previously demonstrated that a small portion of the secondary motor cortex (MOs) in the frontal cortex controls contraversive eye movements, optogenetic suppression of MOs impairs contraversive eye movements, and MOs neurons preferentially encode contraversive eye movements.
evidence: This claim is based on the authors' previous work (Itokazu et al., 2018).

claim: The suppressed eye movement can be recovered over time due to plasticity of the contralateral MOs.
source: Here, we found that the suppressed eye movement can be recovered over time due to plasticity of the contralateral MOs.
evidence: This is the main finding of the current study, supported by experimental data.

claim: The neural representation of motor output is highly plastic even without pathophysiological events.
source: We propose that the neural representation of motor output is highly plastic even without pathophysiological events.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: After several weeks of training, mice became capable of performing eye shifts in the appropriate direction within 10 s to obtain reward with 84.7 ± 2.5% success (n = 10 mice).
source: After several weeks of training, the mice became capable of performing eye shifts in the appropriate direction within 10 s to obtain reward with 84.7 ± 2.5% success (n = 10 mice, See Materials and methods).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral training data from the experiments.

claim: Even though the task required only left eye movement, movements of both eyes were coupled.
source: As we previously reported (Itokazu et al., 2018), even though the task required only left eye movement, movements of both eyes were coupled (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by eye tracking data shown in Figure 1B and previously reported in Itokazu et al., 2018.

claim: 47.0% of imaged MOs neurons showed a significant increase in activity just before eye movement onset (n = 463/985 neurons in ten mice).
source: Among the imaged neurons, 47.0% showed a significant increase in activity just before eye movement onset (n = 463/985 neurons in ten mice).
evidence: This is supported by two-photon calcium imaging data.

claim: Eye movement-related activity is considered a mixture of motor command and visual activity due to the short separation between visual cue onset and motor onset.
source: This activity – which we refer to as eye movement-related activity – is considered a mixture of motor command and visual activity (Itokazu et al., 2018) due to the short separation between visual cue onset and motor onset.
evidence: This is based on the authors' previous work and the experimental design.

claim: The distribution of selectivity was significantly skewed to the positive value, indicating the preference for the contraversive condition as a population.
source: As expected based on our previous report (Itokazu et al., 2018), the distribution of selectivity was significantly skewed to the positive value (Figure 1E and F, Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p<10−10), indicating the preference for the contraversive condition as a population.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of imaging data shown in Figure 1E and F.

claim: More individual neurons showed significantly higher activity in the contraversive eye movement condition (24.5% neurons, contraversive selective) than the ipsiversive one (7.5%, ipsiversive selective).
source: In addition, more individual neurons showed significantly higher activity in the contraversive eye movement condition (24.5% neurons, contraversive selective) than the ipsiversive one (7.5%, ipsiversive selective), confirming that the MOs mainly encodes contraversive eye movement condition.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of individual neuron responses from imaging data.

claim: The MOs mainly encodes contraversive eye movement condition.
source: In addition, more individual neurons showed significantly higher activity in the contraversive eye movement condition (24.5% neurons, contraversive selective) than the ipsiversive one (7.5%, ipsiversive selective), confirming that the MOs mainly encodes contraversive eye movement condition.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the imaging data showing more contraversive-selective neurons.

claim: On the first day of optogenetic suppression, mice could produce contraversive eye movements within a reaction time of 10 s (with suppression: 75.6%, reaction time 1.76 ± 1.47 s, n = 127; without suppression: 85.0%, 1.09 ± 1.72 s, n = 193).
source: On the first day of the optogenetic experiment, although the mice could produce contraversive eye movements within a reaction time of 10 s (with suppression: proportion of trials with a reaction time less than 10 s, 75.6%, reaction time, 1.76 ± 1.47 s, n = 127; without suppression: 85.0%, 1.09 ± 1.72 s, n = 193), they could not during the 1 s suppression period (Figure 2A,B and D; trials with optogenetic suppression: proportion of trials with a reaction time less than 1 s, 7.1%, n = 127; trials without suppression: 40.4%, n = 193 trials; p<10−10, Pearson's chi-square test, see also Itokazu et al. (2018).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2.

claim: On the first day of optogenetic suppression, mice could not produce contraversive eye movements during the 1 s suppression period (with suppression: 7.1% trials with reaction time < 1 s; without suppression: 40.4%; p<10−10).
source: On the first day of the optogenetic experiment, although the mice could produce contraversive eye movements within a reaction time of 10 s (with suppression: proportion of trials with a reaction time less than 10 s, 75.6%, reaction time, 1.76 ± 1.47 s, n = 127; without suppression: 85.0%, 1.09 ± 1.72 s, n = 193), they could not during the 1 s suppression period (Figure 2A,B and D; trials with optogenetic suppression: proportion of trials with a reaction time less than 1 s, 7.1%, n = 127; trials without suppression: 40.4%, n = 193 trials; p<10−10, Pearson's chi-square test, see also Itokazu et al. (2018).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: After several days (5.9 ± 1.0 days, n = 8 mice) of optogenetic suppression, mice regained their contraversive eye movements even during the suppression.
source: However, after several days (5.9 ± 1.0 days, n = 8 mice) of optogenetic suppression, the mice regained their contraversive eye movements even during the suppression (Figure 2C and E; trials with optogenetic suppression: proportion of trials with a reaction time less than 10 s, 90.0%, less than 1 s, 44.5%, reaction time, 1.06 ± 1.00 s, n = 220 trials; trials without suppression: less than 10 s, 90.7%, less than 1 s, 52.7%, 0.78 ± 1.40 s, n = 150 trials; comparison between with and without suppression, p>0.12, Pearson's chi-square test; comparison between suppression on the first day and one on the last day, p<10−12, Pearson's chi-square test), consistent with the behavioral recovery observed in primate lesion studies (van der Steen et al., 1986).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2C and E.

claim: The behavioral recovery observed in mice is consistent with behavioral recovery observed in primate lesion studies.
source: However, after several days (5.9 ± 1.0 days, n = 8 mice) of optogenetic suppression, the mice regained their contraversive eye movements even during the suppression (Figure 2C and E; trials with optogenetic suppression: proportion of trials with a reaction time less than 10 s, 90.0%, less than 1 s, 44.5%, reaction time, 1.06 ± 1.00 s, n = 220 trials; trials without suppression: less than 10 s, 90.7%, less than 1 s, 52.7%, 0.78 ± 1.40 s, n = 150 trials; comparison between with and without suppression, p>0.12, Pearson's chi-square test; comparison between suppression on the first day and one on the last day, p<10−12, Pearson's chi-square test), consistent with the behavioral recovery observed in primate lesion studies (van der Steen et al., 1986).
evidence: This comparison is made to primate studies cited (van der Steen et al., 1986).

claim: The recovery from the initial functional deficit implies that this eye movement might be newly encoded in other brain regions.
source: The recovery from the initial functional deficit implies that this eye movement might be newly encoded in other brain regions.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the behavioral recovery data.

claim: Following optogenetic suppression and recovery, neurons were found that showed a new preference for the ipsiversive movement and those that no longer preferred the contraversive movement.
source: We found neurons that showed a new preference for the ipsiversive movement and those that no longer preferred the contraversive movement (Figure 3D and E).
evidence: This is supported by two-photon imaging data shown in Figure 3D and E.

claim: As a population, many neurons showed an increased preference for the ipsiversive direction or a reduced preference for the contraversive direction (n = 415 eye movement-related neurons in six mice).
source: As a population, many neurons showed an increased preference for the ipsiversive direction or a reduced preference for the contraversive direction (data points below the scatter plot unity line, Figure 3F, n = 415 eye movement-related neurons in six mice), especially for neurons that showed direction-selectivity in the 'before' or 'after' conditions (n = 190 out of 415, black circles).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of imaging data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The distribution for the change in selectivity index was biased toward the ipsiversive condition for direction-selective neurons (p<10−8, Wilcoxon signed-rank test, n = 190).
source: Consistently, the distribution for the change in selectivity index (see Materials and methods) was biased toward the ipsiversive condition for direction-selective neurons (p<10−8, Wilcoxon signed-rank test, n = 190, black bars, top-right inset in Figure 3F), and for all neurons that showed a significant movement-related activity (p<10−6, n = 415, black plus white bars).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of imaging data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The distribution for the change in selectivity index was biased toward the ipsiversive condition for all neurons that showed significant movement-related activity (p<10−6, n = 415).
source: Consistently, the distribution for the change in selectivity index (see Materials and methods) was biased toward the ipsiversive condition for direction-selective neurons (p<10−8, Wilcoxon signed-rank test, n = 190, black bars, top-right inset in Figure 3F), and for all neurons that showed a significant movement-related activity (p<10−6, n = 415, black plus white bars).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of imaging data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: In control mice that expressed only GFP and received no optogenetic suppression, additional training did not cause an increased ipsiversive preference.
source: In control mice that expressed only GFP and thereby received no optogenetic suppression, additional training did not cause an increased ipsiversive preference, but rather led to a tendency for an increased contraversive preference (p=0.13, n = 123 for all direction-selective neurons; p<0.002, n = 282 for all neurons that showed significant motor-related activity, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by control experiment data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: In control mice, additional training led to a tendency for an increased contraversive preference (p=0.13 for direction-selective neurons; p<0.002 for all motor-related neurons).
source: In control mice that expressed only GFP and thereby received no optogenetic suppression, additional training did not cause an increased ipsiversive preference, but rather led to a tendency for an increased contraversive preference (p=0.13, n = 123 for all direction-selective neurons; p<0.002, n = 282 for all neurons that showed significant motor-related activity, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by control experiment data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Optogenetic suppression caused an increase in neurons selective for ipsiversive direction and a decrease in those selective for contraversive direction, accompanied by a learned capacity to make ipsiversive eye movements.
source: Therefore, optogenetic suppression caused an increase in neurons selective for ipsiversive direction and a decrease in those selective for contraversive direction, accompanied by a learned capacity to make ipsiversive eye movements.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing experimental and control data.

claim: On the first day of unilateral suppression, mice were unable to generate contraversive eye movements during 1 s optogenetic suppression (reaction time with suppression: 1.69 ± 1.51 s, n = 35/39 trials vs without suppression: 0.89 ± 1.36 s, n = 92/96 trials, p<0.0002).
source: As expected from Figure 2B, on the first day of unilateral suppression the mice were unable to generate contraversive eye movements during 1 s optogenetic suppression (Figure 4D, reaction time with and without suppression, 1.69 ± 1.51 s, n = 35 out of 39 trials, vs 0.89 ± 1.36 s, n = 92 out of 96 trials, p<0.0002, Mann-Whitney U test, n = 4 mice).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Within several days (3.8 ± 0.7 days), mice regained the capacity to make contraversive movements during unilateral MOs suppression (0.83 ± 0.90 s, n = 59/61 trials vs 0.59 ± 0.90 s, n = 56/61 trials, p>0.07).
source: Within several days (3.8 ± 0.7 days), the mice regained the capacity to make contraversive movements during unilateral MOs suppression (Figure 4B and E, 0.83 ± 0.90 s, n = 59/61 trials vs 0.59 ± 0.90 s, n = 56/61 trials, p>0.07, Mann-Whitney U test).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4B and E.

claim: Additional suppression of the MOs in the contralateral hemisphere caused the same impairment as on the first day (1.27 ± 1.21 s, n = 35/37 trials vs 0.45 ± 0.97 s, n = 102/108 trials, p<10−5).
source: However, additional suppression of the MOs in the contralateral hemisphere caused the same impairment as on the first day (Figure 4C and F, 1.27 ± 1.21 s, n = 35/37 trials vs 0.45 ± 0.97 s, n = 102/108 trials, p<10−5, Mann-Whitney U test).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4C and F.

claim: The reaction time for bilateral suppression was significantly longer than that for post-training unilateral suppression (1.27 ± 1.21 s vs. 0.83 ± 0.90 s, p<0.02).
source: The reaction time for bilateral suppression was significantly longer than that for post-training unilateral suppression (Figure 4E and F, bottom, 1.27 ± 1.21 s vs. 0.83 ± 0.90 s, p<0.02, Mann-Whitney U test), and was similar to the reaction time before training (first day, Figure 4D bottom, 1.69 ± 1.51 s, p>0.05, Mann-Whitney U test).
evidence: This is supported by statistical comparison of behavioral data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The reaction time for bilateral suppression was similar to the reaction time before training (bilateral: 1.27 ± 1.21 s; first day: 1.69 ± 1.51 s, p>0.05).
source: The reaction time for bilateral suppression was significantly longer than that for post-training unilateral suppression (Figure 4E and F, bottom, 1.27 ± 1.21 s vs. 0.83 ± 0.90 s, p<0.02, Mann-Whitney U test), and was similar to the reaction time before training (first day, Figure 4D bottom, 1.69 ± 1.51 s, p>0.05, Mann-Whitney U test).
evidence: This is supported by statistical comparison of behavioral data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The trial proportion with a reaction time less than 1 s was 21.6 ± 8.1% (n = 4 mice) for bilateral suppression, which was significantly lower than that for unilateral suppression (56.0 ± 9.7%, p<0.001).
source: The trial proportion with a reaction time less than 1 s was 21.6 ± 8.1% (n = 4 mice) for bilateral suppression, which was significantly lower than that for unilateral suppression (56.0 ± 9.7%, p<0.001, Pearson's chi-square test), but similar to that before training (10.6 ± 5.2% for before training, p>0.25, Pearson's chi-square test).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: The trial proportion with a reaction time less than 1 s for bilateral suppression was similar to that before training (bilateral: 21.6 ± 8.1%; before training: 10.6 ± 5.2%, p>0.25).
source: The trial proportion with a reaction time less than 1 s was 21.6 ± 8.1% (n = 4 mice) for bilateral suppression, which was significantly lower than that for unilateral suppression (56.0 ± 9.7%, p<0.001, Pearson's chi-square test), but similar to that before training (10.6 ± 5.2% for before training, p>0.25, Pearson's chi-square test).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: The significant impact of the bilateral suppression demonstrates that the contralateral MOs acquired an essential role in motor recovery after repetitive optogenetic suppression.
source: The significant impact of the bilateral suppression demonstrates that the contralateral MOs acquired an essential role in motor recovery after repetitive optogenetic suppression.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the bilateral suppression experiment data.

claim: The essential role of contralateral MOs, together with new encoding for ipsiversive direction, suggests that the dynamic properties of MOs neurons may underlie suppression-induced adaptation.
source: This essential role, together with new encoding for ipsiversive direction (Figure 3), suggests that the dynamic properties of MOs neurons may underlie suppression-induced adaptation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from combining the bilateral suppression and imaging results.

claim: This is the first direct evidence showing dynamic directional encoding of eye movement across hemispheres.
source: To our knowledge, this is the first direct evidence showing dynamic directional encoding of eye movement across hemispheres.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the findings based on the authors' knowledge of the literature.

claim: The recovery process following unilateral optogenetic suppression shares similarity with recovery processes following a unilateral lesion in the motor cortex in human patients and in animal models.
source: Our finding unveiled a recovery process following unilateral optogenetic suppression. It shares similarity with recovery processes following a unilateral lesion in the motor cortex in human patients and in animal models (reviewed in Alia et al., 2017; Murphy and Corbett, 2009; Nudo, 2007).
evidence: This comparison is made to lesion studies cited in reviews.

claim: Cortical lesions are usually induced by events such as cortical resection, aspiration, traumatic brain injuries, and experimental strokes, which severely damage neurons, glial cells, vessels, neighboring axons, and the extracellular matrix including perineuronal nets.
source: Cortical lesions are usually induced by events such as cortical resection, aspiration, traumatic brain injuries, and experimental strokes, which severely damage neurons, glial cells, vessels, neighboring axons, and the extracellular matrix including perineuronal nets.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about cortical lesions.

claim: Cortical damage initiates highly complex pathophysiologic reactions like inflammation and reactive gliosis, which leads to the upregulation of neurotrophic factors and pro-inflammatory cytokines.
source: This damage initiates highly complex pathophysiologic reactions like inflammation and reactive gliosis, which leads to the upregulation of neurotrophic factors and pro-inflammatory cytokines.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about pathophysiological responses to brain damage.

claim: All pathophysiological reactions following cortical damage could, in principle, be involved in plasticity.
source: All of these reactions could, in principle, be involved in plasticity (Alia et al., 2017; da Silva Meirelles et al., 2017; Fawcett, 2015; Li et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: It was not clear whether functional recovery could be achieved without complex pathophysiological events triggered by cortical lesions.
source: Therefore, it was not clear whether functional recovery could be achieved without complex pathophysiological events triggered by cortical lesions.
evidence: This identifies a gap in knowledge that the study addresses.

claim: A built-in plastic capability of normal cortical circuits alone could cause motor recovery of eye movement.
source: Our findings demonstrate that a built-in plastic capability of normal cortical circuits alone could cause motor recovery of eye movement.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings showing recovery without lesion-induced pathophysiology.

claim: The motor cortex in the contralateral hemisphere underlies the flexibility in the neural representation of motor output.
source: Our findings demonstrate that the motor cortex in the contralateral hemisphere underlies the flexibility in the neural representation of motor output.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: Studies in the forelimb/hindlimb motor cortex suggest that both the perilesional areas and the contralateral unaffected motor cortex play critical roles in motor recovery.
source: Studies in the forelimb/hindlimb motor cortex suggest that both the perilesional areas and the contralateral unaffected motor cortex play critical roles in motor recovery (Alia et al., 2017; Benowitz and Carmichael, 2010; Murphy and Corbett, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Following a cortical lesion, neurons in the contralateral cortex show increased turnover of dendritic spines and an increased number of dendritic branches.
source: In particular, following a cortical lesion, neurons in the contralateral cortex show increased turnover of dendritic spines and an increased number of dendritic branches.
evidence: This is based on established findings in the field.

claim: Following a large unilateral infarct, pharmacological silencing of the contralateral hemisphere can deteriorate recovered forelimb movement, indicating a facilitatory role.
source: Consistently, following a large unilateral infarct, pharmacological silencing of the contralateral hemisphere can deteriorate recovered forelimb movement, indicating a facilitatory role (Biernaskie et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Biernaskie et al., 2004.

claim: The role of the contralateral hemisphere in motor recovery remains controversial.
source: However, the role of the contralateral hemisphere still remains controversial (Alia et al., 2017; Hosp and Luft, 2011; Mohajerani et al., 2011), and indeed a study showed that silencing the undamaged contralateral hemisphere by continuous infusion of GABA-A agonist improves recovery performance, implying a suppressive role (Mansoori et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies showing conflicting results.

claim: Silencing the undamaged contralateral hemisphere by continuous infusion of GABA-A agonist improves recovery performance, implying a suppressive role.
source: However, the role of the contralateral hemisphere still remains controversial (Alia et al., 2017; Hosp and Luft, 2011; Mohajerani et al., 2011), and indeed a study showed that silencing the undamaged contralateral hemisphere by continuous infusion of GABA-A agonist improves recovery performance, implying a suppressive role (Mansoori et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Mansoori et al., 2014.

claim: A prevailing hypothesis is that the role of the contralateral hemisphere depends on the size of infarction, particularly on whether remaining intact cortical areas in the ipsi-lesional hemisphere can take over the original functions of the lesioned area.
source: A prevailing hypothesis that reconciles these findings is that the role of the contralateral hemisphere depends on the size of infarction, particularly on whether remaining intact cortical areas in the ipsi-lesional hemisphere can take over the original functions of the lesioned area (Buetefisch, 2015; Di Pino et al., 2014).
evidence: This hypothesis is supported by citations to Buetefisch, 2015 and Di Pino et al., 2014.

claim: If remaining intact cortical areas in the ipsi-lesional hemisphere can take over the original functions, they will be interfered with by the contralateral hemisphere.
source: If they can, they will be interfered with by the contralateral hemisphere.
evidence: This is part of the hypothesis about the role of the contralateral hemisphere.

claim: If remaining intact cortical areas in the ipsi-lesional hemisphere cannot take over the original functions, the contralateral hemisphere can substitute for the functions of the lesioned area.
source: If they cannot, the contralateral hemisphere instead can substitute for the functions of the lesioned area.
evidence: This is part of the hypothesis about the role of the contralateral hemisphere.

claim: Neighboring areas in the hemisphere ipsilateral to the optogenetic suppression may not substitute for the role of MOs in the eye movement task.
source: Our findings suggest that neighboring areas in the hemisphere ipsilateral to the optogenetic suppression, despite potentially exhibiting some forms of plasticity, may not substitute for the role of MOs in our task.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental findings showing the importance of the contralateral hemisphere.

claim: The MOs has a latent capability to control ipsiversive eye movements and can learn to turn on these movements.
source: Our findings indicate that the MOs has a latent capability to control ipsiversive eye movements and can learn to turn on these movements.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the imaging and behavioral data.

claim: The latent capability of MOs to control ipsiversive eye movements might depend on existing anatomical projections from the MOs to subcortical eye-movement related regions for ipsiversive movements.
source: This capability might depend on existing anatomical projections from the MOs to subcortical eye-movement related regions for ipsiversive movements.
evidence: This is speculation about the anatomical basis for the observed plasticity.

claim: The MOs normally projects to the superior colliculus.
source: For instance, the MOs normally projects to the superior colliculus.
evidence: This is based on established anatomical knowledge.

claim: Projections from MOs to the contralateral superior colliculus are rather sparse.
source: However, in this case the MOs likely would need to project to the contralateral superior colliculus; these projections are rather sparse (Oh et al., 2014, for example, mouse #141603190).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Oh et al., 2014 and reference to specific anatomical data.

claim: There are relatively strong projections from the MOs to the contralateral striatum.
source: Another possibility is the relatively strong projections from the MOs to the contralateral striatum (Oh et al., 2014); the striatum has been linked to saccade output as an indirect pathway in primates (Basso and Sommer, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Oh et al., 2014.

claim: The striatum has been linked to saccade output as an indirect pathway in primates.
source: Another possibility is the relatively strong projections from the MOs to the contralateral striatum (Oh et al., 2014); the striatum has been linked to saccade output as an indirect pathway in primates (Basso and Sommer, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Basso and Sommer, 2011.

claim: Optogenetic suppression has been a standard technique to investigate the specific functions of neural circuits.
source: Optogenetic suppression has been a standard technique to investigate the specific functions of neural circuits (Guo et al., 2014; Li et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Guo et al., 2014 and Li et al., 2016.

claim: Repeated suppression across multiple days can induce changes in the functions of the contralateral hemisphere, leading to the recovery from the initial motor deficits induced by optogenetic suppression.
source: Our data show that repeated suppression across multiple days can induce changes in the functions of the contralateral hemisphere, leading to the recovery from the initial motor deficits induced by optogenetic suppression.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: The impact of optogenetic suppression needs to be interpreted with caution, and the suppression paradigms need to be carefully designed.
source: Therefore, our results indicate that the impact of optogenetic suppression needs to be interpreted with caution, and the suppression paradigms need to be carefully designed.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the findings of the study.

claim: The study highlights the flexibility of cortical circuits that can overcome even short-term reversible manipulation of neural activity.
source: Our study highlights the flexibility of cortical circuits that can overcome even short-term reversible manipulation of neural activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.
